analysis.one_liner: Exempts logging and forestry work from Clean Water Act discharge permits.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have freed logging operations from federal water pollution permits, never left a House subcommittee and died when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed the Clean Water Act so that discharges from forestry work — logging, site preparation, road building, prescribed burns, pest control, and tree nurseries — would no longer need a federal water pollution permit. It would also rewrite the law's definition of "point source" so logging stormwater runoff wouldn't count as a regulated discharge. The bill was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its water subcommittee, where it stayed until Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Timber companies, forest landowners, and logging operators would gain if the bill passed: they would no longer need National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permits for runoff from harvesting, forest roads, site preparation, and related work, cutting their compliance costs and paperwork.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new section to the Clean Water Act stating that no permit is required under the discharge permit program for discharges from forestry activities, including site preparation, reforestation, thinning, prescribed burning, pest and fire control, harvesting, surface drainage, road construction and maintenance, and nursery operations.

Rewrites the Clean Water Act's definition of "point source" so that stormwater runoff from those forestry activities is excluded, alongside the existing exclusions for agricultural stormwater and irrigation return flows.

analysis.who_pays: People living downstream of logging operations would bear the cost: streams, rivers, and lakes receiving sediment and pollution from forestry runoff would no longer be covered by the federal discharge permitting system, leaving water quality protections weaker.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities and waterways downstream of logging

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the federal permit requirement for the full range of logging activities, including harvesting and road construction and maintenance, which are sources of sediment-laden runoff into streams; it excludes that runoff from the Clean Water Act's definition of "point source."

Because the exemption applies to discharges of stormwater runoff from all listed forestry activities, states and water agencies downstream would lose a federal backstop for addressing pollution from those sources.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a clear cost saving to the timber industry by lifting permitting requirements, but the trade-off is weaker federal control of runoff from logging roads and harvest sites — a known source of sediment and pollution in streams. Whether the burden on waterways is justified by reduced paperwork depends on whether state-level protections could fill the gap, and the bill as written simply removes the federal permit requirement without adding anything in its place.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its water subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on February 9, 2000 by Rep. Max Sandlin, joined by Reps. Turner and Berry.
It was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, and that is the last recorded action on the bill.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever recorded, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, the Clean Water Act's permitting requirements for forestry runoff stayed in place, and downstream communities kept the existing federal water quality protections that the bill would have removed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Downstream water users kept existing protections

for.name: Rep. Max Sandlin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt forestry activities from Clean Water Act discharge permits.

for.name: Reps. Jim Turner and Marion Berry
for.what_they_did: Joined Rep. Sandlin in introducing the bill on the House floor.

for.name: 6 House cosponsors (3 Democrats, 3 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors after introduction.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referring the bill to its Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — the three original introducers were Democrats and the six cosponsors split evenly, 3 Democrats and 3 Republicans — but no vote was ever taken, so no voting pattern exists.

industries.note: The bill would have exempted logging, forest road construction, and related activities from federal water discharge permits, saving the industry compliance costs while removing a federal check on sediment and pollutant runoff into streams. The public cost would be weaker protection of the waters downstream of logging operations.

Nursery operations were explicitly listed among the activities exempt from permitting, so nursery operators would have been freed from discharge permit requirements. The corresponding cost falls on water quality downstream.
